title: Prevalence of Schistosoma mansoni infection among children in Ethiopia: a systematic review and meta-analysis

subsections.subsection_title: Public Health Response and Control Strategies in Ethiopia
subsections.content: Ethiopia has implemented a national schistosomiasis control program centered on mass drug administration (MDA) with praziquantel, aligned with World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines targeting school-aged children as the primary at-risk group. The national mapping initiative conducted between 2013 and 2015 provided critical epidemiological data, revealing a 3.5% prevalence of Schistosoma mansoni among schoolchildren and guiding targeted MDA deployment in endemic woredas, particularly in western and northeastern regions ref [2]. Diagnostic strategies during this mapping phase optimized sensitivity through pooled stool examination techniques, enhancing cost-efficiency and scalability for large-scale surveillance ref [5]. Despite progress, coverage remains suboptimal, with challenges in drug delivery, community compliance, and sustained funding limiting the impact of MDA alone ref [1]. In response, Ethiopia is increasingly integrating schistosomiasis control with other neglected tropical disease programs and WASH (water, sanitation, and hygiene) interventions to address transmission drivers holistically. Recent policy frameworks emphasize moving beyond chemotherapy toward integrated, community-based approaches that include environmental modification and health education, reflecting global calls for sustainable elimination strategies ref [1].

subsections.subsection_title: Risk Factors and Determinants of Infection
subsections.content: The risk of Schistosoma mansoni infection among children in Ethiopia is strongly influenced by behavioral, environmental, and socioeconomic determinants. Poor personal hygiene practices, including infrequent handwashing before meals and after defecation, significantly increase infection risk, as demonstrated in a study from Medebay Zana wereda where these behaviors were associated with adjusted odds ratios of 9.0 and 5.77, respectively ref [4]. Similarly, consumption of unwashed vegetables was identified as a key risk factor, with an AOR of 5.67 ref [4]. Environmental exposure to contaminated freshwater sources remains a critical determinant, particularly in regions where children swim, bathe, or wash clothes in rivers inhabited by infected snails; in Sanja Town, such activities were strongly correlated with S. mansoni infection prevalence of 89.9% ref [5]. Additionally, open defecation near water bodies and walking barefoot in endemic areas further facilitate transmission ref [4]. Socioeconomic factors, particularly low maternal education, have also been linked to higher infection rates, likely due to reduced health literacy and inadequate sanitation practices ref [4]. These determinants collectively underscore the need for integrated interventions targeting hygiene promotion, access to clean water, and community-based sanitation infrastructure.

subsections.subsection_title: Global and Regional Burden of Schistosoma mansoni
subsections.content:
Schistosoma mansoni is a major contributor to the global burden of schistosomiasis, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, where it remains one of the most prevalent neglected tropical diseases. In 2013, an estimated 261 million people required preventive chemotherapy for schistosomiasis, with 92% of this burden concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa, yet only 12.7% of at-risk individuals received treatment ref [7]. The disease is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality, with annual deaths in Africa alone estimated at up to 280,000 ref [7]. Schistosomiasis ranks second only to malaria in terms of parasitic disease burden in the region, contributing to 57 million disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) lost annually across all neglected tropical diseases ref [6]. Children are disproportionately affected, with chronic infection impairing cognitive development, school performance, and physical growth, thereby perpetuating cycles of poverty ref [6].

Despite global efforts, including the World Health Assembly’s Resolution WHA65.21 calling for 75% treatment coverage of school-age children by 2020, implementation remains inadequate, with schistosomiasis showing the lowest levels of preventive chemotherapy coverage among all neglected tropical diseases ref [7]. The Schistosomiasis Control Initiative (SCI), launched in 2002, has played a pivotal role in scaling up mass drug administration in several African countries, yet coverage gaps persist due to limited resources, weak health systems, and persistent transmission in endemic areas ref [8]. While progress has been made in countries like Brazil, China, and Egypt toward elimination, most sub-Saharan nations continue to struggle with sustained control ref [6]. The formation of the Global Schistosomiasis Alliance in 2015 aimed to galvanize coordinated action, but challenges in funding, political commitment, and surveillance infrastructure hinder progress ref [7].

subsections.subsection_title: Epidemiology and Prevalence of S. mansoni in Ethiopian Children
subsections.content: Schistosoma mansoni infection remains a significant public health concern among school-aged children in Ethiopia, with prevalence rates varying substantially across regions. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 94 studies reported a national pooled prevalence of 18.0% (95% CI: 14.0–23.0), with the southern region exhibiting a higher burden at 25.9% (95% CI: 14.9–41.1) ref [9]. Regional cross-sectional studies further highlight this heterogeneity, with prevalence reaching 44.8% in Southwest Ethiopia (Mizan-Aman) ref [12], 37.9% in Zarima Town (Northwest) ref [16], and 79.5% among boys in Sanja Town (Amhara) ref [11], underscoring localized transmission hotspots. Urban settings are not exempt, as evidenced by a study in Jimma town reporting substantial infection rates despite urbanization, indicating expanding transmission dynamics ref [13]. Gender disparities are consistent, with males showing higher infection rates in multiple studies, likely due to increased water contact behaviors ref [10]. Age-related trends indicate higher prevalence among children aged 5–14 years, with peak infection intensities observed in younger schoolchildren ref [11]. A baseline survey in Ejaji found a 12.94% prevalence, with swimming and river bathing identified as key risk factors ref [14], while in rural Bahir Dar, prevalence was 8.0% but significantly higher among children using river water for domestic purposes ref [10]. Overall, despite national control efforts, S. mansoni continues to disproportionately affect children in endemic areas, particularly those with limited access to clean water and sanitation.

subsections.subsection_title: Prevalence of Schistosoma mansoni infection among school children in Ethiopia
subsections.content:
The prevalence of Schistosoma mansoni infection among school children in Ethiopia varies significantly across regions, reflecting differences in water contact behaviors, sanitation infrastructure, and socioeconomic conditions. In Sanja Town, Northwest Ethiopia, a cross-sectional study reported an alarmingly high prevalence of 89.9% among school children, with swimming in contaminated rivers and washing clothes or utensils in river water identified as key risk factors ref [5]. Similarly, in Medebay Zana wereda, Tigray, the overall prevalence of intestinal helminths was 12.7%, with S. mansoni being the most prevalent species, strongly associated with poor hand hygiene, open defecation, and consumption of unwashed vegetables ref [4]. These findings underscore the role of environmental exposure and behavioral practices in transmission dynamics. Regional disparities are further evident in other studies, where prevalence ranges from below 10% in low-risk zones to over 80% in endemic riverine communities. The high burden in school-aged children highlights the need for targeted school-based interventions, including mass drug administration and health education, particularly in areas with limited access to clean water and sanitation facilities.

Geospatial and ecological factors, such as proximity to freshwater bodies and seasonal flooding, further modulate infection rates. In areas where riverine activities are integral to daily life, transmission persists despite national control efforts. Integrated approaches combining chemotherapy, behavioral change communication, and WASH (water, sanitation, and hygiene) improvements are essential to reduce the persistent burden of S. mansoni among Ethiopian school children.

subsections.subsection_title: Diagnostic Methods and Mapping Strategies in Ethiopia
subsections.content:
The national mapping of Schistosoma mansoni infection in Ethiopia has primarily relied on the Kato-Katz (KK) thick smear technique, which remains the gold standard for stool-based diagnosis due to its low cost and feasibility in resource-limited settings. However, its sensitivity is limited in low-intensity infection settings, prompting evaluations of alternative tools. A pivotal study by Leta et al. compared individual and pooled stool examination strategies during Ethiopia’s national mapping, demonstrating that pooled Kato-Katz significantly improved diagnostic efficiency and cost-effectiveness without substantial loss in sensitivity, making it suitable for large-scale surveys ref [3].

In recent years, the point-of-care circulating cathodic antigen (POC-CCA) urine test has emerged as a valuable complementary tool, particularly for detecting low-intensity infections in areas where prevalence has declined due to control efforts. Multiple SCORE-funded evaluations have validated the POC-CCA assay for mapping S. mansoni across varying prevalence levels, highlighting its utility in identifying residual infections missed by KK, especially in pre-elimination contexts ref [17]. While not without limitations—such as variability in reading and potential false positives—the POC-CCA has been increasingly integrated into Ethiopia’s surveillance framework to enhance mapping accuracy and inform targeted interventions.

Geospatial mapping strategies have further refined targeting by correlating infection hotspots with environmental and demographic factors. Although primarily applied in Sierra Leone, the methodological framework using model-based geostatistics to link S. mansoni prevalence with elevation and population density offers a transferable model for Ethiopia’s diverse ecological zones ref [5]. Together, these diagnostic and mapping innovations are enabling a more precise, data-driven approach to schistosomiasis control in Ethiopia.

Praziquantel (PZQ) coverage among school-age children (SAC) in Ethiopia remains suboptimal, with national estimates indicating that only 75.5% of targeted children received treatment in 2019, despite mass drug administration (MDA) programs being in place ref [19]. Coverage varied significantly by district, with integrated treatment approaches—combining schistosomiasis and soil-transmitted helminth interventions—achieving 87.5% coverage compared to 72.5% under vertical programs (p < 0.001) ref [19]. Factors such as school enrollment (AOR = 20.90), male sex (AOR = 1.27), and older age (10–14 years; AOR = 1.45) were strongly associated with higher PZQ uptake ref [19].

The efficacy of PZQ against Schistosoma mansoni in Ethiopian children remains high, with a pooled cure rate of 86.65% (95% CI: 83.4–93.9) and an egg reduction rate exceeding 87% across multiple studies ref [20]. Subgroup analyses revealed slightly higher cure rates in Amhara (88.58%) than in Oromia (84.79%), suggesting regional variations in treatment response, possibly due to transmission intensity or drug delivery logistics ref [20]. Despite high heterogeneity (I² = 93.4%), no evidence of clinical resistance was detected, and infection prevalence dropped from 55.77% to 11.29% post-treatment ref [20]. These findings support the continued use of standard-dose PZQ as a cornerstone of Ethiopia’s schistosomiasis control strategy, though improved coverage and monitoring are critical to sustain efficacy and move toward elimination.

subsections.subsection_title: National Control Programs and Progress Toward Elimination
subsections.content:
Ethiopia has made significant strides in its national control program for schistosomiasis, aligning with the World Health Organization’s 2012 roadmap for neglected tropical diseases. By 2015, the Federal Ministry of Health achieved 100% mass drug administration (MDA) coverage in all schistosomiasis-endemic districts, leveraging integrated NTD programming and strong political commitment. This progress was supported by partnerships with international agencies such as the Schistosomiasis Control Initiative and RTI International, which facilitated resource mobilization and logistics for praziquantel distribution to school-aged children and at-risk communities. Despite these achievements, challenges persist in sustaining coverage and ensuring treatment adherence, as highlighted by the global critique that current MDA-only strategies yield limited long-term impact due to low compliance and reinfection rates ref [1].

Ethiopia’s 2020 elimination targets for schistosomiasis were ambitious, and while MDA coverage reached near-universal levels in mapped areas, the absence of complementary interventions—such as water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) infrastructure and snail control—limits the potential for true elimination ref [1]. The country’s NTD Master Plan recognized the need for an integrated approach, yet implementation of non-pharmaceutical components remains fragmented. Recent evaluations suggest that without addressing socioenvironmental determinants and strengthening health systems, gains from MDA may be transient. Continued investment in surveillance, community engagement, and cross-sectoral collaboration is essential to transition from control to sustainable elimination.

Socioenvironmental and geospatial determinants play a critical role in the transmission dynamics of Schistosoma mansoni among children in Ethiopia. Access to safe water and adequate sanitation remains a key protective factor, with meta-analytic evidence showing that improved sanitation reduces the odds of S. mansoni infection by 41% (OR=0.59, 95% CI: 0.47–0.73) ref [22]. In eastern Ethiopia, community-level awareness gaps significantly increase infection risk, with individuals unaware of transmission routes or prevention methods being over five times more likely to be infected ref [4]. Behavioral factors, particularly frequent water contact through swimming or bathing in contaminated rivers, are strongly associated with higher infection rates (adjusted OR=6.41) ref [4]. Spatial analyses reveal that high local population density within 1 km of residential areas correlates with increased transmission, likely due to intensified contamination of freshwater sources ref [24]. Malacological surveys confirm the presence of Biomphalaria pfeifferi snails—essential intermediate hosts—in all major water contact points in endemic kebeles, reinforcing the link between environmental suitability and infection hotspots ref [4]. Additionally, seasonal flooding and proximity to slow-moving rivers or irrigation canals further amplify exposure risk, particularly in rural and peri-urban settings where infrastructure is limited.

Geospatial modeling in Ethiopia has identified clustering of infections near lakes, rivers, and dams, with transmission intensity varying significantly across agro-ecological zones. These patterns underscore the need for targeted, location-specific interventions that integrate environmental monitoring with community education and WASH (water, sanitation, and hygiene) improvements to disrupt transmission cycles effectively.

subsections.subsection_title: Regional Prevalence of S. mansoni in Ethiopian Children
subsections.content:
The regional prevalence of Schistosoma mansoni infection among children in Ethiopia varies significantly across endemic zones, reflecting heterogeneous environmental and socioecological conditions. The southern region exhibits the highest pooled prevalence at 25.9% (95% CI: 14.9–41.1), surpassing the national average of 18.0%, likely due to favorable climatic conditions for intermediate snail hosts and high water contact rates ref [9]. Amhara and Oromia regions account for the majority of survey sites, with adjusted prevalence rates exceeding 50% in 36.8% of locations, indicating intense transmission hotspots ref [5]. In contrast, regions such as Tigray and the Afar lowlands report substantially lower prevalence, often below 10%, attributed to arid conditions and limited aquatic habitats for Biomphalaria snails ref [5]. School-based studies further confirm elevated infection rates in rural, riverside communities, particularly in the Rift Valley and western lowlands, where access to clean water and sanitation remains limited ref [10]. Gender disparities are less pronounced in children compared to adults, though some regional analyses suggest slightly higher infection rates among boys due to increased water-related activities ref [10].

Geospatial mapping reveals a strong correlation between S. mansoni prevalence and elevation (847–2,100 m), vegetation index, and proximity to permanent freshwater bodies, reinforcing the biogeographical determinants of transmission ref [5]. Despite national control efforts, persistent hotspots in southern and western Ethiopia underscore the need for targeted, regionally tailored interventions to achieve elimination goals.

Funding for schistosomiasis control and research in Ethiopia has been primarily driven by international partnerships and donor-funded initiatives, with the Schistosomiasis Control Initiative (SCI) playing a pivotal role in scaling up preventive chemotherapy and mapping efforts ref [25]. The Ethiopian government, in alignment with national NTD roadmaps, has increasingly mobilized domestic resources to complement external funding, particularly through the Ministry of Health’s integrated neglected tropical disease programs ref [14]. Multilateral agencies such as the World Bank and the Global Fund have supported large-scale school-based deworming campaigns, enabling sustained praziquantel distribution to school-age children ref [1]. However, funding gaps persist, particularly in remote endemic zones where health infrastructure is weak and surveillance systems under-resourced ref [15]. Recent studies highlight that inconsistent funding cycles have undermined longitudinal monitoring and the transition from control to elimination phases ref [10]. Moreover, the adoption of point-of-care diagnostic tools like the CCA urine assay has been constrained by limited financial allocation for new technologies, despite their superior sensitivity in low-prevalence settings ref [15]. Strengthening local financial stewardship and integrating schistosomiasis funding into broader health financing frameworks remains critical for sustainability ref [25].

Innovative financing models, including results-based financing and public-private partnerships, have been piloted in select regions but lack nationwide scalability due to insufficient policy support and data infrastructure ref [14]. Community-based funding mechanisms, though promising, remain underdeveloped and rarely integrated into national budgeting processes.
